paragraphs: Reinforcement learning policies often work well on their training tasks but struggle when task demands change. This paper examines how much of a policy network actually needs to change during adaptation. Its theoretical analysis, formulated for Markov Decision Processes, shows that adapting linear layers before and after a policy backbone can be sufficient.

The resulting Adaptive Policy Backbone keeps the central network frozen and learns lightweight, task-specific linear transformations on either side. The input transformation changes what reaches the backbone, while the output transformation adjusts how its representation produces actions. This concentrates task adaptation in a small part of the architecture rather than updating the entire policy.

The reported results show performance comparable to standard reinforcement learning while learning only these surrounding layers, even with a randomly initialized backbone. The authors also find that this structural restriction can improve generalization, including on out-of-distribution tasks where representative meta-learning approaches struggle. Together, the findings support a simpler architecture for adaptation and show that a learned, task-specific backbone is not always required for strong performance.
icml-2026-adaptive-policy-backbone-via-s.tldr: Adapting linear layers around a frozen policy backbone can match standard reinforcement learning performance and improve task generalization.

paragraphs: A language model can encode the correct answer internally yet still choose the wrong option on a multiple-choice question. This paper studies that mismatch as a knowledge-prediction gap. The distinction matters because an incorrect response may reflect a failure to use available information, rather than an absence of that information in the model.

The authors first measure how prevalent and substantial the gap is across models and datasets. They then analyze the residual stream, the internal representations through which information passes across the model. Their geometric account identifies separate subspaces associated with knowledge and prediction, giving a concrete representation-level description of how the two can become misaligned.

KAPPA is a lightweight intervention applied during inference that aligns these subspaces within the residual stream. The reported results show that it reduces the gap across multiple-choice benchmarks and models, with generalization to free-form settings. The contribution combines an interpretable account of the mismatch with a practical intervention aimed at making outputs more faithful to information already represented internally.
icml-2026-bridging-the-knowledge-predict.tldr: KAPPA aligns internal knowledge and prediction subspaces to help language models use answers they already encode.

paragraphs: Federated learning must learn from data distributed across clients, where privacy and differences between local datasets complicate class balancing. Underrepresented classes can consequently receive poor predictions. FedCGNM addresses this problem through the optimizer used on each client, changing how updates from different class groups contribute to learning.

The method partitions classes into a small number of groups using a minimum within-group variance criterion. It maintains momentum for each group, normalizes each momentum vector to unit length, and sums those vectors to determine the update direction. This equalizes the magnitude of majority- and minority-group contributions while reducing noise in rare-class gradients. The convergence analysis explicitly includes resampling rates that change over time.

A second method, FedHOO, searches for useful resampling rates in small-client settings. Its bandit-based search exploits federated parallelism to evaluate many combinations of two candidate rates per client at linear cost. Across four public long-tailed benchmarks and a chip-defect dataset, FedCGNM consistently outperforms the evaluated baselines; FedHOO supplies additional gains in small federations.
icml-2026-class-grouped-normalized-momen.tldr: FedCGNM balances class-group updates in federated learning, while FedHOO efficiently tunes resampling rates for smaller federations.

paragraphs: Multi-objective reinforcement learning asks a policy to handle several goals that may conflict. A max-min criterion promotes fairness by focusing on the worst-performing objective, rather than allowing strong results on some objectives to overshadow weak results on others. This paper addresses how to combine that criterion with explicit constraints on acceptable behavior.

The proposed framework makes constraint satisfaction part of the multi-objective learning problem. That matters because balancing objectives and respecting constraints are distinct requirements: a fair balance alone does not establish that a policy meets its restrictions. The authors develop a theoretical foundation and analyze convergence of the resulting algorithm, alongside experiments in tabular settings.

They also evaluate the approach in simulated building thermal control, multi-objective locomotion, and traffic management that accounts for greenhouse-gas emissions. Across these domains, the reported results show effective balancing of fairness and constraint satisfaction. The contribution connects a fairness-oriented objective to constrained decision-making, with theoretical support in the analyzed setting and practical demonstrations across several types of control problem.
icml-2026-constrained-multi-objective-re.tldr: This framework combines max-min fairness with explicit constraints in multi-objective reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: This paper separates three ingredients that are often entangled: the underlying world, the process that generates training data, and the representations a model learns. Its controlled world consists of 5,075 city coordinates, with seven geometric tasks producing data for autoregressive Transformers. This makes it possible to compare representations while keeping the underlying world fixed.

Training on different individual tasks produces distinct representation geometries. With multiple tasks, however, models develop more aligned representations, even when their training tasks do not overlap. The authors interpret this as controlled evidence for the Multitask Scaling Hypothesis within the Platonic Representation Hypothesis: learning multiple tasks can encourage convergence toward a shared representation of the world.

The adaptation findings reveal a separate difficulty. After pretraining on all tasks and cities, the authors test whether fine-tuning can integrate new entities consistently. Some tasks actively damage this integration, despite the benefits of multitask pretraining. The results therefore distinguish representational convergence from successful expansion: an aligned world representation can still be vulnerable to divergent tasks when new entities are introduced.
icml-2026-convergent-world-representatio.tldr: Multitask training aligns learned world representations, but some fine-tuning tasks can severely disrupt the integration of new entities.

paragraphs: Scientific simulation requires models to predict how a system evolves, often over long periods. Euler–Poincaré Neural Dynamics approaches this by learning evolution through Lie-group flows, a geometric description of structured transformations. Geometry becomes part of the model's architecture, shaping how it represents temporal change.

This formulation provides a principled way to handle curvature, symmetry, and conservation when learning an evolution operator. The intended advantage is that temporal propagation follows an explicitly geometric framework instead of being represented solely as an unconstrained input-output map. That connects the learned dynamics to mathematical structure relevant to scientific systems.

The paper also introduces an Euler–Poincaré Parallel Scan to make this formulation computationally scalable. It uses the associativity of Lie-group compositions, allowing transformations to be grouped for parallel computation rather than processed entirely in sequence. The authors report high accuracy, strong stability, and substantial parallel acceleration across scientific simulations of long-horizon dynamics. The contribution brings together a structured model of evolution and an algorithm that exploits the same structure to accelerate computation.
icml-2026-eulerpoincare-neural-dynamics-.tldr: Euler–Poincaré Neural Dynamics combines geometric evolution models with parallel computation for accurate, stable long-horizon simulation.

paragraphs: Classical neural-network approximation results often assume exact arithmetic over real numbers. Computer implementations instead use a finite set of floating-point values and operations that introduce rounding. This paper asks what networks can represent when both those numerical restrictions and the actual automatic-differentiation procedure are included in the analysis.

The authors study a network composed with a given floating-point function, such as a loss. They show that the network can represent arbitrary target function values while automatic differentiation of the composition represents arbitrary target input gradients. The gradient statement concerns the output of the automatic-differentiation algorithm, which is central to the paper's treatment of implemented computation.

The result extends to several outer functions: under mild conditions, one network can represent the target values while their respective differentiated compositions simultaneously represent arbitrary gradients. The findings apply to practical activations including ReLU, GELU, sigmoid, and tanh. This establishes expressive-power results that explicitly incorporate machine arithmetic and automatic differentiation, rather than relying on the exact-real assumptions of earlier function-and-gradient approximation theory.
icml-2026-floating-point-networks-with-a.tldr: The paper establishes broad representability results for floating-point network values and automatically computed gradients, including simultaneous gradients under mild conditions.

paragraphs: Many sampling methods operate on finite-dimensional vectors, but some problems naturally ask for entire functions or trajectories. Sampling diffusion paths subject to rare events or boundary constraints is one motivation. This paper develops a learning-based sampler directly for infinite-dimensional function spaces, where theory and algorithm design have been less developed.

The Functional Adjoint Sampler targets Gibbs-type distributions on Hilbert spaces. It extends Adjoint Sampling using stochastic optimal control, with the stochastic maximum principle providing the theoretical basis. This leads to a matching-style training objective for a functional representation, connecting the function-space formulation to a simple and scalable learning procedure.

The authors evaluate transition path sampling in synthetic potential systems and molecular systems, including Alanine Dipeptide and Chignolin, and report superior performance. These results support the usefulness of extending sampling beyond a finite-vector formulation when the objects of interest are trajectories. The contribution is both a theoretical generalization of adjoint sampling and a concrete algorithm demonstrated on systems with meaningful transition paths.
icml-2026-functional-adjoint-sampler-sca.tldr: The Functional Adjoint Sampler extends control-based diffusion sampling to function spaces and improves reported transition path sampling performance.

paragraphs: Unsupervised reinforcement learning pretrains policies to perform different skills without task-provided rewards, creating a starting point for later control tasks. This paper identifies two obstacles in existing off-policy approaches: the meaning of a skill changes during learning, and the resulting policies can generalize poorly when downstream conditions differ.

GenDa addresses the changing meaning of skills through a relabeling mechanism. By revising skill labels, it mitigates this non-stationarity and improves the efficiency of pretraining data use. The method also introduces a Complementary Information Bottleneck, which encourages the policy to emphasize ego-centric features—features centered on the agent—and become more robust to distribution shifts.

These components address different parts of the same goal: learning reusable skills efficiently and retaining their usefulness beyond pretraining conditions. Across the reported experiments, GenDa improves sample efficiency and generality, supporting more scalable unsupervised reinforcement learning. The findings suggest that skill learning benefits from treating both evolving skill semantics and downstream robustness as explicit design problems within a unified framework.
icml-2026-learning-generalizable-skill-p.tldr: GenDa combines skill relabeling with an information bottleneck to improve unsupervised skill learning efficiency and generalization.

paragraphs: A multimodal model judging an answer may favor a convincing explanation even when it conflicts with the image. The authors call this Perceptual Judgment Bias. Through controlled visual perturbations, they show that existing judges frequently anchor on response text instead of visual evidence, making their evaluations inconsistent and difficult to verify.

To train against this failure, they construct the Perceptually Perturbed Judgment Dataset. Minimally edited counterfactual responses isolate perceptual errors, supplying supervision whose correctness can be checked against the visual evidence. The training framework combines a structured GRPO-based reward with a batch-ranking objective, encouraging coherent ordering across responses without requiring explicit pairwise labels.

Across diverse multimodal judging benchmarks, the approach substantially improves fidelity to visual evidence, consistency of rankings, and agreement with human evaluations. These findings connect the diagnosed bias to a targeted training intervention: isolate visual mistakes, then reward judgments that recognize them. The authors present this as a scalable route toward interpretable judges that are more robust when persuasive reasoning and visual evidence disagree.
icml-2026-mitigating-perceptual-judgment.tldr: Targeted counterfactual training helps multimodal judges prioritize visual correctness over persuasive but perceptually wrong responses.

paragraphs: Transformer expressivity is often analyzed under exact arithmetic, where parameters and operations use real numbers without rounding. This paper studies the different setting of floating-point parameters and machine operations. Its focus is on which functions such Transformers can represent and which permutation symmetries survive numerical computation.

Permutation equivariance means that rearranging input elements produces the corresponding rearrangement of outputs. The authors show that floating-point Transformers can represent functions without this property even when positional encodings are absent. They also prove that all permutation-equivariant functions can be represented for bounded sequence lengths, while this universality fails when sequence length becomes large.

The analysis identifies a minimal equivariance property that remains in floating-point Transformers. It further shows that every non-trivial additive positional encoding can harm representability. This is a possibility statement about expressive power, rather than a claim that positional encoding always worsens task performance. Together, the results show that exact-arithmetic accounts of Transformer symmetry and representability cannot simply be transferred to implemented floating-point models.
icml-2026-on-expressive-power-of-floatin.tldr: Floating-point arithmetic changes Transformer expressivity, including permutation symmetry, sequence-length limits, and the effects of positional encoding.

paragraphs: How small can a neural network be while still representing every function on its input domain? Existing answers often assume exact real-number arithmetic. This paper instead studies ReLU networks whose parameters and operations use floating-point numbers, asking about exact representation of functions from floating-point vectors to floating-point outputs.

For the full domain and codomain considered, the minimum depth is exactly three. Two layers can suffice when the input domain, output codomain, or both are smaller. The minimum width for inputs with d components falls between 2d and 2d+4, giving a narrow range rather than a single exact width threshold.

Restricting inputs to non-negative floating-point numbers changes the width bounds to between d and d+4. Smaller domains can permit still narrower networks, including widths below d. These results show that domain restrictions materially affect the architecture needed for universal representation. More broadly, they establish that minimum-size results derived with exact arithmetic do not automatically carry over to networks operating with machine rounding.
icml-2026-on-minimum-depth-and-width-of-.tldr: Floating-point ReLU networks require depth three for full-domain universal representation, with minimum width tightly bounded by input dimension.

paragraphs: Language models increasingly act in environments where decisions affect later outcomes, but their original training does not directly prepare them for online decision-making. This paper introduces Iterative Regret-Minimization Fine-Tuning, a post-training procedure that repeatedly teaches a base model from decision trajectories with low regret.

Regret serves as a signal of decision quality, guiding which behavior is distilled into the model. The procedure incorporates natural-language reasoning generated by the model itself. It therefore provides a way to train decision behavior without requiring imitation of a known decision algorithm or a manually prescribed reasoning format.

The reported improvements span numerical Transformers, lightweight open-weight language models, and GPT-4o mini. The trained behavior also generalizes across different interaction horizons, action spaces, reward processes, and scenarios described in natural language. These findings support regret as a useful signal for post-training decision agents across varied settings. The authors nevertheless frame the method as an initial exploration, motivating further development of principled post-training approaches specifically suited to decision-making.
icml-2026-post-training-llms-as-better-d.tldr: Repeatedly fine-tuning on low-regret trajectories improves decision-making across several model types and decision settings.

paragraphs: Linear attention represents a sequence through an evolving memory state, enabling inference time that grows linearly with sequence length. Existing key-value approaches typically use queries only to read this memory. Q-Delta examines whether queries can also supply useful information for updating the state itself.

The authors show that query-conditioned readout produces a structured prediction of values from accumulated memory, complementing key-based retrieval. Their query-aware delta rule combines key- and query-based prediction errors when updating the state. This lets both sources contribute corrections while retaining the efficiency associated with delta-rule updates.

The paper establishes stability guarantees for these dynamics and derives a chunkwise-parallel formulation, implemented with custom Triton code for hardware efficiency. Experiments report stable optimization, competitive throughput, and consistent improvements over strong baselines in language modeling and long-context retrieval. The contribution links a change in the role of queries to both an analyzed update rule and a practical implementation, showing benefits from making readout information part of memory evolution.
icml-2026-q-delta-beyond-keyvalue-associ.tldr: Q-Delta uses query- and key-based prediction errors to improve recurrent memory updates while preserving efficient linear attention.

paragraphs: Useful prediction intervals must balance two goals: include the true value often enough and remain narrow enough to be informative. QpiGNN addresses this tradeoff for graph neural networks, where dependencies in graph data complicate uncertainty estimation and reliable intervals can require expensive resampling or calibration.

Building on quantile regression, the method directly optimizes interval coverage and width without requiring quantile inputs or post-processing. A dual-head architecture separates prediction from uncertainty, and a joint loss trains both using label-only supervision. This makes interval quality an explicit training objective instead of leaving uncertainty entirely to a later calibration stage.

The theory provides asymptotic coverage and near-optimal interval-width guarantees under mild assumptions. Across 19 synthetic and real-world benchmarks, the authors report average coverage that is 22% higher and intervals that are 50% narrower than those of the evaluated baselines. They also report efficiency and robustness to noise and structural shifts. These empirical results support the joint objective, while the theoretical guarantees remain conditional and asymptotic.
icml-2026-quantile-free-uncertainty-quan.tldr: QpiGNN directly learns graph prediction intervals, reporting improved coverage and narrower widths without quantile inputs or post-processing.

paragraphs: Model merging combines separately fine-tuned models into one model with capabilities across tasks. Data-free merging must decide which parameter changes to retain without using task data. This paper argues that simple parameter-level rules overlook dependencies between layers and the uneven distribution of expertise within a network.

SA-Merging assigns saliency scores to task vectors, the changes from a shared base model, using connectivity-based ideas from structural pruning. It also adjusts these scores according to agreement among experts to reduce interference between tasks. An iterative procedure removes non-informative updates while preserving end-to-end connectivity, so selection accounts for how updates participate in the larger network.

The method extends to low-rank adapters through rank-wise saliency decomposition that preserves their structural integrity. Experiments on vision and language tasks demonstrate the approach's effectiveness and reduce the performance gap between data-free merging and test-time adaptation methods. The central contribution is a more structured criterion for combining expertise: evaluate update importance through connectivity and expert agreement rather than relying only on isolated parameter heuristics.
icml-2026-saliency-aware-model-merging-8.tldr: SA-Merging combines task-specific models using connectivity-aware saliency and expert agreement, with support for low-rank adapters.

paragraphs: Large training batches often bring diminishing returns or worse performance in reinforcement learning because the policy and its data distribution keep changing. This paper argues that the amount of change varies during training. Early behavior shifts rapidly, while later learning can approach a more stable regime where larger batches become useful.

Adaptive Batch Scaling adjusts the effective batch size according to measured policy stability. Its Behavioral Divergence metric tracks changes in actions between consecutive updates. Batch size scales inversely with that volatility: more behavioral change calls for smaller batches, while a more stable policy permits larger batches and more precise convergence.

The authors integrate this mechanism with Parallelised Q-Network and evaluate it on the ALE benchmark. In those experiments, combining larger networks with larger batches achieves the best performance under adaptive batch control. The finding challenges a fixed view of batch-size limits in reinforcement learning: useful batch sizes depend on the evolving learning dynamics. The evidence supports adapting computation to policy stability in the evaluated algorithm and benchmark.
icml-2026-scalable-reinforcement-learnin.tldr: Adaptive Batch Scaling increases batch size as policy behavior stabilizes, enabling stronger scaling results with larger networks on ALE.

paragraphs: Evaluating three-dimensional seismic fault detection requires both trustworthy labels and data that resemble real surveys. SeisMark is an open benchmark designed to bring these properties together. Its motivation is that simplified physics data can conceal weaknesses that become visible when models encounter more realistic seismic textures.

The benchmark is generated through a pipeline combining procedural geology with diffusion-based synthesis. Procedural structure supplies verifiable ground truth, while synthesis produces textured volumes tailored to survey-specific domains. This creates an evaluation setting that connects known geological structure with realistic appearance, allowing robustness to domain changes to be examined more directly.

The reported experiments show that SeisMark distinguishes a robust modern architecture from a legacy model whose performance collapses under realistic domain shifts. The benchmark therefore contributes an evaluation resource that exposes brittleness hidden by simpler data. Its release is intended to support development of trustworthy models for safety-critical subsurface applications, with verifiable labels and realistic texture serving as complementary requirements for assessing progress.
icml-2026-seismark-a-large-scale-open-be.tldr: SeisMark combines verifiable geology with realistic seismic textures to expose fault-detection failures under domain shifts.

paragraphs: Sharpness-Aware Minimization seeks flatter loss minima by evaluating an update gradient at a nearby perturbed point. This paper identifies a mismatch that can arise: the gradient at that nearby point can vanish even though the gradient at the current parameters remains nonzero. SAM can then stall where the original loss is not stationary.

The authors call these points hallucinated minimizers. They prove that such points exist for some perturbation distances under simple nonconvex landscape conditions, including the presence of a local minimum and a local maximum. They also establish sufficient conditions for SAM iterates to converge locally to these points, showing that the issue can affect optimization dynamics rather than merely being a geometric possibility.

Neural-network experiments corroborate the failure mode, which aligns with the performance deterioration often observed at large perturbation distances. A short initial phase of ordinary stochastic gradient descent before switching to SAM mitigates the problem and reduces sensitivity to the perturbation distance. This is a practical safeguard supported by the reported observations, rather than a claim that warm-starting eliminates every such failure.
icml-2026-sharpness-aware-minimization-c.tldr: SAM can converge to nonstationary points of the original loss, and a short SGD warm-start mitigates this failure mode.

paragraphs: Sleep recordings contain structure at very different timescales, from short signal patterns to the organization of an entire night. SleepMaMi is a foundation model designed to learn both. It addresses the tendency of task-specific approaches to emphasize local features while overlooking full-night structure and the multiple signals in polysomnography.

A hierarchical design assigns these scales to two encoders. The Macro-Encoder learns overnight temporal dependencies through contrastive training guided by subject metadata such as age and sex. The Micro-Encoder captures short-term biosignal characteristics through a combination of masked reconstruction and multimodal contrastive learning. These objectives give the model complementary ways to learn global sleep patterns and local signal morphology.

Pretraining uses more than 20,000 polysomnography recordings, totaling 158,000 hours. Across a diverse set of downstream tasks, SleepMaMi matches or exceeds existing foundation models and demonstrates stronger generalizability and label-efficient adaptation. The results support combining full-night context with fine-grained signals in a shared foundation model for clinical sleep analysis, rather than treating each timescale as an isolated modeling problem.
icml-2026-sleepmami-a-universal-sleep-fo.tldr: SleepMaMi learns full-night sleep structure and short-term biosignal patterns together, supporting generalizable and label-efficient downstream analysis.

paragraphs: Mixture-of-Experts models activate only selected experts for each input, making the router central to useful specialization. This paper argues that a shallow linear routing projection has limited awareness of input structure and can lead to unstable assignments. STAR adds an explicit mechanism for tracking that structure.

The method augments learned routing with an evolving principal subspace that captures dominant patterns in input representations. It updates this subspace using the Generalized Hebbian Algorithm. Routing decisions can therefore draw on a continually tracked account of input structure, helping experts develop stable specialization around the inputs they receive.

Evaluations include a controlled synthetic setting and large-scale language and vision tasks. STAR consistently improves routing quality and downstream performance over the strong MoE baselines tested. Optional subspace updates at test time further improve robustness and generalization when input distributions shift. The contribution treats routing as both a learned assignment rule and a representation-learning problem, with the evolving subspace supplying structural information that supports expert selection.
icml-2026-star-rethinking-moe-routing-as.tldr: STAR tracks dominant input structure to stabilize expert routing and improve performance, with optional adaptation under test-time distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Applying language-model techniques to tables raises a basic representation problem: numbers carry relationships that ordinary tokenization can obscure. Nearby numerical values should retain a sense of proximity, and their ordering also matters. TabularBERT addresses these properties when turning numerical variables into inputs for a Transformer.

The model uses binning-based tokenization, discretizing numerical variables into groups of values. It learns representations that account for numerical proximity and order, while masked self-supervised pretraining captures conditional dependencies among variables. These are complementary goals: preserve meaningful relationships within a numerical column and learn how information across columns relates.

The authors report empirical evidence of effectiveness and interpretability. Their contribution focuses on adapting the representation machinery of language models to structured numerical data, where treating values as ordinary tokens can lose useful information. The findings highlight the potential of this approach for tabular representation learning while recognizing that classical machine-learning methods already achieve substantial success on structured data. The key design choice is to make numerical structure part of the learned representation.
icml-2026-tabularbert-binning-based-self.tldr: TabularBERT combines numerical binning with masked Transformer pretraining to learn tabular representations that account for proximity, order, and cross-variable dependencies.

paragraphs: Language-model agents can lose track of their goals during extended interaction, even when their immediate reasoning appears strong. Multi² addresses this objective drift through a hierarchy of complementary agents. The design separates deciding what subgoal to pursue from selecting the individual actions needed to carry it out.

The high-level agent, called System 1, uses supervised fine-tuning to generate subgoals appropriate to the current context. The low-level agent, System 2, learns atomic actions through reinforcement learning that moves from offline to online interaction. This division assigns planning and execution distinct roles and training procedures, supporting sustained control and efficient adaptation.

Across diverse interactive environments, Multi² consistently outperforms the strong agentic baselines evaluated, with better robustness and coordination over multiple turns. The authors also release three hierarchical benchmark datasets for training and evaluating this kind of decision-making. Together, the framework and datasets address both how to organize long-horizon agents and how to study that organization, with the reported results supporting hierarchy as a way to mitigate goal drift.
icml-2026-texttt-multi-2-hierarchical-mu.tldr: Multi² separates subgoal planning from action execution to improve sustained interaction and reduce objective drift in language-model agents.

paragraphs: Understanding a model's internal geometry requires deciding what makes two representations meaningfully different. This paper argues that the answer should reflect how representations produce behavior. It focuses on representations that define softmax probability distributions, proposing information geometry as the natural framework for studying their semantic structure.

The analysis connects this geometry to semantic encoding and the linear representation hypothesis. Its practical application is dual steering, which uses linear probes to guide representations toward a target concept. The method links concept manipulation to the geometry of the distributions produced by the model, making behavioral consequences central to the intervention.

The authors prove that dual steering optimally modifies the target concept while minimizing changes to off-target concepts within their formulation. Empirically, it improves the controllability and stability of concept manipulation. The contribution therefore combines a proposed geometric account with an intervention grounded in that account. Its stated scope is the important case of softmax-defined representations, where changes in internal states can be understood through changes in output distributions.
icml-2026-the-information-geometry-of-so.tldr: Dual steering uses the information geometry of softmax representations to target concepts while minimizing off-target changes.

paragraphs: This paper identifies an internal token interface in video language models: a continuous representation space in which visual tokens can function as entities within the architecture. V-LynX uses that interface as an entry point for additional sensory inputs, drawing on structure the video model has already learned.

The framework adds a lightweight auxiliary pathway alongside a frozen vision encoder. It aligns both attention responses and statistical distributions using unpaired, single-modality datasets. The goal is to make new inputs compatible with the existing token interface while integrating the model's video priors, avoiding dependence on heavy modality-specific encoders or paired supervision.

The authors report state-of-the-art performance and efficiency across audio-visual question answering, 3D reasoning, high-frame-rate video, and multi-view video understanding benchmarks. These results support the interface as a reusable component for extending video models across sensory settings. The central contribution is to treat a model's internal visual-token organization as something new modalities can align with, providing a common integration mechanism across several forms of input.
icml-2026-v-lynx-token-interface-alignme.tldr: V-LynX aligns new sensory inputs with a video model's existing token interface using a lightweight pathway and unpaired data.
